av_event.what: As she says 'they're getting older', her smile drops and she looks away to her left towards the window for two or three seconds, pressing her lips together, then looks back at the camera before 'so'.

text:
A: Hello! Hi, sorry, can you hear me? I think it's working.
B: Yes, I can hear you. Hello.
A: Oh, good. I'm Agnieszka, I'm in Basingstoke. Sorry, it's a long name, people just say Aga sometimes.
B: I'm Helen. Otley, near Leeds.
A: Ah, Yorkshire! Did you find the puzzle okay? I was so worried I was doing it wrong, I checked the instructions about three times.
B: Erm, it was alright. The last one took me a while. I think I overthought it.
A: Me too, exactly the same! So, what do you do, if you don't mind me asking?
B: I'm an archivist. At a university library in Leeds, special collections. Three days a week.
A: Oh, that's interesting. So like old documents, letters?
B: Yes, mostly. Letters, diaries, estate papers. I catalogue them so people can actually find what's there. And I supervise the reading room some days. It's quiet work, which suits me, if that makes sense.
A: It makes total sense. I'm executive assistant to a finance director, sorry, Chief Financial Officer, at insurance company. So his diary, board papers, travel. Not so quiet! But I like it. I've been with him six years now, I know exactly how he wants everything.
B: Six years is a long time with one person. You must know his handwriting by now.
A: Oh, his handwriting is terrible! Honestly, I'm the only one in office who can read it. People bring me his notes like I'm translator.
B: That's half my job, really. Seventeenth-century handwriting is probably not so different from a finance director's.
A: Ha, maybe! Do you have family up there?
B: My daughter, Isla. She's nine. And my mum's nearby, she helps with the school pick-up.
A: Oh, my daughter is nine as well! Zosia. Year Four?
B: Year Four, yes.
A: That's so funny. She has swimming on Thursdays and Polish school on Saturdays, so I'm like a taxi, you know?
B: Polish school, that's good. Does she like it?
A: Mostly. Sometimes she complains. But I want her to talk properly with my parents, they're in Rzeszów, they don't speak much English. I fly back twice a year but, erm, they're getting older, so.
B: Is it far? From the airport, I mean.
A: Not bad, there's a flight from Luton straight to Rzeszów. Two hours. I'm always at airport much too early, Tomasz, my husband, he laughs at me.
B: I'd be the same. I like knowing where I'm meant to be.
A: Yes! Everything in one plastic folder, passports, everything.
B: That's not daft. I lost a boarding pass in Norway once, years ago. Never again.
A: Norway! Was it beautiful?
B: It was. The Lofoten Islands. Before Isla. I'd like to take her one day, when she's old enough to walk properly without moaning.
A: Oh, that sounds lovely. We usually do Croatia or Portugal, with another Polish family. Very easy, kids play, we sit.
B: That sounds quite relaxing, actually.
A: It is. Sorry, I'm talking a lot, is that okay?
B: It's fine. I'm not much of a talker, so it helps.
A: Okay, good! I think we have maybe one minute?
